title: Celsus the Epicurean contradicts himself
source_text: Ἔοικε δὲ μετὰ δεινότητος συναγορεύειν πως τοῖς μαρτυροῦσι τῷ χριστιανισμῷ μέχρι θανάτου λέγων· καὶ οὐ τοῦτο λέγω, ὡς χρὴ τὸν ἀγαθοῦ δόγματος περιεχόμενον, εἰ μέλλει δι᾿ αὐτὸ κινδυνεύειν παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις, ἀποστῆναι τοῦ δόγματος ἢ πλάσασθαι ὡς ἀφέστηκεν ἢ ἔξαρνον γενέσθαι. καὶ καταγινώσκει γε τῶν φρονούντων μὲν τὰ χριστιανισμοῦ προσποιουμένων δὲ μὴ φρονεῖν ἢ ἀρνουμένων, λέγων μὴ δεῖν τὸν ἐν τῷ δόγματι πλάσασθαι ὡς ἀφέστηκεν ἢ ἔξαρνον αὐτοῦ γενέσθαι. ἐλεγκτέον δὴ ὡς τὰ ἐναντία ἑαυτῷ λέγοντα τὸν Κέλσον. εὑρίσκεται μὲν γὰρ ἐξ ἄλλων συγγραμμάτων Ἐπικούρειος ὤν· ἐνταῦθα δὲ διὰ τὸ δοκεῖν εὐλογώτερον κατηγορεῖν τοῦ λόγου μὴ ὁμολογῶν τὰ Ἐπικούρου προσποιεῖται κρεῖττόν τι τοῦ γηΐνου εἶναι ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ συγγενὲς θεοῦ καί φησιν ὅτι οἷς τοῦτο εὖ ἔχει, τουτέστιν ἡ ψυχὴ, πάντη ἐφίεται τοῦ συγγενοῦς, λέγει δὲ τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ ἀκούειν ἀεί τι (καὶ) ἀναμιμνήσκεσθαι περὶ ἐκείνου ποθοῦσιν. ὅρα οὖν τὸ νόθον αὐτοῦ τῆς ψυχῆς, ὅτι προειπὼν, ὡς χρὴ τὸν ἀγαθοῦ δόγματος περιεχόμενον, καὶ εἰ μέλλει δι᾿ αὐτὸ κινδυνεύειν παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις, μὴ ἀφίστασθαι τοῦ δόγματος μηδὲ πλάσασθαι ὡς ἀφέστηκε μηδ᾿ ἔξαρνον γενέσθαι, αὐτὸς τοῖς ἐναντίοις πᾶσι περιπίπτει. ᾔδει γὰρ ὅτι ὁμολογῶν Ἐπικούρειος εἶναι οὐκ ἂν ἔχοι τὸ ἀξιόπιστον ἐν τῷ κατηγορεῖν τῶν ὅπως ποτὲ πρόνοιαν εἰσαγόντων καὶ θεὸν ἐφιστάντων τοῖς οὖσι. δύο δὲ παρειλήφαμεν Κέλσους γεγονέναι Ἐπικουρείους, τὸν μὲν πρότερον κατὰ Νέρωνα τοῦτον δὲ κατὰ Ἀδριανὸν καὶ κατωτέρω.
pass_a_gloss: He seems with cleverness (δεινότης) somehow to plead on behalf of (συναγορεύω) those bearing witness (μαρτυρέω) to Christianity until death, saying: 'and I do not say this, that one who holds (περιέχομαι) a good doctrine (ἀγαθὸν δόγμα), if he is about to be endangered (κινδυνεύω) on account of it among men, must stand away from (ἀφίστημι) the doctrine or feign (πλάσσομαι) that he has stood away or become a denier (ἔξαρνος).' And he condemns (καταγινώσκω) those who think the things of Christianity but pretend (προσποιέομαι) not to think them or deny (ἀρνέομαι), saying that the one in the doctrine must not feign he has stood away or become a denier of it. He must be refuted as saying things contrary (ἐναντία) to himself. For he is found from other writings (συγγράμματα) to be an Epicurean (Ἐπικούρειος); but here, for the sake of seeming to accuse (κατηγορέω) the teaching more reasonably, not confessing (ὁμολογέω) the things of Epicurus, he pretends that there is something better (κρεῖττον) than the earthly (γήϊνος) in man, akin (συγγενής) to God, and says that those for whom this is well (εὖ ἔχει) — that is, the soul (ψυχή) — it strives (ἐφίεμαι) in every way for the kindred, he means God, and they long (ποθέω) always to hear something and to be reminded (ἀναμιμνήσκομαι) about that one. See then the bastardy/spuriousness (τὸ νόθον) of his soul: that having said beforehand that one who holds a good doctrine, even if he is about to be endangered on account of it among men, must not stand away from the doctrine nor feign he has stood away nor become a denier, he himself falls into (περιπίπτω) all the contraries. For he knew that confessing to be an Epicurean he would not have trustworthiness (ἀξιόπιστον) in accusing those who in whatever way introduce (εἰσάγω) providence (πρόνοια) and set God over (ἐφίστημι) the things that are (τὰ ὄντα). We have received (παραλαμβάνω) that there were two Celsuses, Epicureans, the earlier under Nero, this one under Hadrian and later (κατωτέρω).
pass_b_english: With some cleverness he seems in a way to speak up for those who bear witness to Christianity even to death, when he says: “And I do not say that a man who holds to a good doctrine ought, if he is going to be in danger among men because of it, to abandon the doctrine, or pretend that he has abandoned it, or deny it.” And he condemns those who hold the beliefs of Christianity but pretend not to hold them, or deny them, saying that one who holds the doctrine ought not to pretend that he has abandoned it, or deny it.

We must show, then, that Celsus contradicts himself. From other writings of his he is found to be an Epicurean. But here, so that his accusation of our teaching may seem more reasonable, he does not admit to the views of Epicurus. Instead he pretends that there is in man something better than the earthly, akin to God, and he says that in those in whom this is in good health (that is, the soul), “it reaches out in every way toward what is akin to it” (he means God), “and they long always to hear something about him and to be reminded of him.”

See, then, how counterfeit his soul is. Having said beforehand that a man who holds to a good doctrine, even if he is going to be in danger among men because of it, must not abandon the doctrine, nor pretend that he has abandoned it, nor deny it, he himself falls into every one of the opposite faults. For he knew that if he admitted he was an Epicurean, he would have no credibility in accusing those who, in whatever way, teach a providence and set God over all that exists. We have learned that there were two Epicureans named Celsus: the earlier under Nero, and this one under Hadrian and later.

choices.choice: Celsus's first sentence is direct speech (first person λέγω) and is quoted. His second statement is reported (φησιν ὅτι), but its phrasing is his; Origen's glosses ('that is, the soul', 'he means God') are kept outside the quotation marks. Koetschau's '(καὶ)' before ἀναμιμνήσκεσθαι is an editorial insertion, translated ('and to be reminded'). Grammar: in 'οἷς τοῦτο εὖ ἔχει ... πάντη ἐφίεται' the singular verb takes τοῦτο (the soul) as subject, while ποθοῦσιν is plural ('they long'); rendered accordingly. Celsus's first form is negative ('I do not say that a man ought to abandon'); Origen's restatement is a prohibition ('must not abandon', with 'even if'); both kept as the Greek frames them. 'Martyrs' is avoided for μαρτυροῦσι, rendered 'bear witness ... even to death'. 'God' is capitalized for the supreme God Celsus here speaks of, as Origen glosses it. 'τὸ νόθον αὐτοῦ τῆς ψυχῆς' rendered 'how counterfeit his soul is'. No Scripture in this chapter.
